items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: although I studied some with him... I studied with him for a while... he turned me over to who was his star pupil, Rudy Powell

ctx.x: Now what kind of sound, I mean, you were listening to some of these records, but what kind of sound did he encourage you to try for on the Alto?

Well, the sound ... I don't remember exactly what he encouraged me to try for, but I was sort of after the sound of Frankie Trumbauer at that time, and if you're familiar with Rudy Powell, which you certainly must be, you know, Rudy is a very fine saxophone player, and although I studied some with him, and then with Lieutenant Mikel Michael, our sounds were, you know, quite different.

items.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: His assistant was Rudy Powell, who came to be known later as a very great, fine lead player with some of the orchestras around that time.

ctx.x: Can you remember any of the other people that you worked with early on?

Actually, the teacher that he recommended first was a professor, Eugene Michaels, who had been in the army or whatever service, some military service, and, considering I was a beginner, he had his assistant teach me and spend as much time with me as Professor Michaels himself did. His assistant was Rudy Powell, who came to be known later as a very great, fine lead player with some of the orchestras around that time.
Let’s see. Did we mention . . . we didn’t mention Arthur Reeves at all?
